newsitem.title: GERMANY: GERMAN CALL MONEY STAYS FIRM ON REPO SPECULATION.
newsitem.headline: GERMAN CALL MONEY STAYS FIRM ON REPO SPECULATION.

text.p: German call money rates remained firm at 3.12/3.15 percent on Friday as banks speculated the Bundesbank may switch to variable-rate tenders for securities repurchase agreements next week.
Dealers said some banks were hoarding funds in the expectation that the Bundesbank may signal higher interest rates next week in defence of the mark. That was why market liquidity remained tight.
"The money is there but no one is being coaxed out into the market with it," one dealer said.

Call money rates were likely to remain firm at least until next Tuesday, when the Bundesbank is scheduled to set its next weekly repo auction and reveal what form the tender will take -- fixed-rate, variable-rate, or a combination of both.
"If the Bundesbank sets unchanged fixed repos at 3.00 percent, call money will rapidly fall to 3.05 percent," one money dealer said. The repo rate has been fixed at 3.00 percent since August 1996.
Dealers are speculating that the Bundesbank may opt for a variable repo tender, in which the repo rate is determined by the rates at which banks bid for central bank funds.
Some say the Bundesbank may set a two-week variable repo alongside a four-week fixed repo tender to provide a ceiling for rates and prevent banks from bidding the rate too high.

Commercial banks' effective deposits at the Bundesbank -- a measure of market liquidity -- fell to 40.0 billion marks on Thursday from 41.2 billion marks. Average deposits for the month fell to 40.7 billion marks from 40.8 billion.
Banks' borrowings from the Lombard borrowings fell to about 0.3 billion marks from 0.6 billion marks.
The Frankfurt Interbank Overnight Average (FIONA) - was 3.15600 percent, up from 3.14108 percent.
